GoPi worker — the task worker loop (a plain temporary process).

One loop round (the contract):
  ① claim the next pending task (atomic CAS — a lost claim race yields to
     the next round, so two workers never double-run one row);
  ② execute it through the standard task-run machinery (child gopi run);
  ③ terminal state lands via the must-succeed push — every sync peer is
     told the terminal status (no worker-side push code);
  ④ 顺势 db-sync: one pull-then-push session per peer (pull first, then
     push — our rows land on the peer's freshest state);
  ⑤ claim the next task. A drained queue does NOT hold the worker
     forever: it waits (GOPI_WORKER_IDLE_SEC, default 30s) and re-checks,
     and after GOPI_WORKER_IDLE_EXITS (default 3) consecutive empty rounds
     it exits 0 on its own — a worker is a task-drain tool that runs and
     self-dies, not a daemon. '--once' drains then exits 0 immediately.

Usage:
  gopi worker                    # run the task-management loop; self-exits
                                 # after N idle rounds on a drained queue
  gopi worker --once             # run until the queue drains, then exit 0
  gopi worker --daemon           # same loop, DETACHED: the command returns
                                 # immediately with the new pid; the worker
                                 # keeps the drain-and-self-die contract
  gopi worker -h | --help        # this help (claims NOTHING — zero side-effects)

Detached mode (--daemon):
  The flag changes WHO owns the terminal AND adds the single-instance guard:
  at most ONE detached worker daemon may run per profile, so a second
  --daemon is refused (it names the holder's pid). The loop itself is
  unchanged — it still executes the same claim→run→sync rounds and, without
  GOPI_WORKER_IDLE_EXITS=0, still drains and self-exits. Its stdout/stderr
  go to <gopi-dir>/logs/worker.log, and the launcher prints pid + that path.

Privileges (--daemon):
  A detached worker needs NO privilege: start it as the ordinary user you
  already are. Running it as root does not obtain the escape either — a
  process inherits its cgroup from its launcher, so a privileged daemon was
  measured in the SAME login session scope, and root has no user manager of
  its own to migrate into (both measured).
  When the escape is unavailable the start says so and the daemon runs
  anyway: setsid already removes the controlling-terminal exposure, and what
  remains is that it ends with the session scope. --require-scope turns that
  degradation into a refused start when you need the guarantee rather than
  the convenience. For a start that outlives the login session, a host's own
  service unit is the operator's lever — not a password.
  NEITHER the foreground loop NOR '--once' detaches: '--once' is the
  foreground drain of the queue (claim -> run -> push -> sync until drained,
  then exit 0) — the ONE task 'gopi task run next' claims, applied repeatedly,
  plus the round/idle bookkeeping around it. Reach for '--once' where you
  would otherwise loop 'gopi task run next' yourself. Nothing is spawned and
  no cgroup is touched, so it needs no privilege either.

Resident daemon management (--status / --stop / --restart / --start):
  --daemon is the ONLY spelling that takes the single-instance lock: two
  DETACHED workers can never run at once (a second --daemon is refused with
  the holder's pid), while a FOREGROUND 'gopi worker' still needs no lock —
  run one in the front to watch it, any time.

  gopi worker --status           # ANSWER + WHY: one line per LIVE worker (pid,
                                 # idle|busy, task + session); when there is
                                 # none, WHAT that means and how to start one.
                                 # Then a labelled block for the state files
                                 # that are NOT workers (dead-pid SIGKILL
                                 # residue), with the count, a bounded sample
                                 # and the command that clears them. Worker =
                                 # state file OR argv shape, so a FOREGROUND
                                 # worker (no lock, no state file) is listed
                                 # too. READ-ONLY: takes no lock, creates
                                 # nothing.
  gopi worker --status-verbose   # the same report with EVERY residue path
                                 # listed (the default samples a few of them)
  gopi worker --stop             # finish the in-flight round, then exit
                                 # [--wait 25m] [--force]
  gopi worker --restart          # --stop then --start, atomically
  gopi worker --start            # start a detached daemon (refused if one runs)

  The stop request is a durable per-pid file AND a signal (SIGTERM): either
  alone is enough, so a missed signal cannot strand a daemon. --force adds
  SIGUSR1 (interrupt the round now).

Loop cap:
  GOPI_WORKER_MAX_ROUNDS=N       max claim→run→sync rounds before exit
                                 (default 0 = unlimited; malformed/negative
                                 falls back to the default with a warning).

Drained-queue wait:
  GOPI_WORKER_IDLE_SEC=N         seconds between re-checks on a drained
                                 queue (default 30; --once exits instead)

Idle self-exit:
  GOPI_WORKER_IDLE_EXITS=N       consecutive empty rounds before the worker
                                 exits 0 on its own (default 3 ≈ 90s of
                                 quiet; 0 = wait forever, kill to stop)

Queue exclusion:
  rows tagged "pa-queue" are NEVER claimed by the worker loop — the same
  fixed anti-misclaim guard the serve daemon's --skip-tag enforces
  (human/other-dispatcher handling only).
